column1: # Step 2: the nine ways to fake this step, priced at the whole of it.
# These are standing rules -- no id begins `m<digit>-`, so score.py reads them
# as preconditions rather than as a share of the reward -- and they are the only
# standing rules whose failure costs *both* families. That is what the file is
# for: score.py reads the ids out of this file by name, so "which reds zero the
# whole step" is the contents of one file rather than a list in the scorer that
# can drift away from the rules it names.
# `Encoders.kryo` is the reason the file exists. Handing an opaque
# `StructureDataInterface` to the SQL engine through a Kryo encoder produces a
# Dataset, a terminal action, and a real SQL execution id on the job --
# measured, not supposed (NOTES 6.2.5, the seventh shape). Every job rule of
# m02.tsv goes green on it, and so does the `-rdd-gone` half, because the RDD
# count really is gone. What it does not produce is a migration: the engine sees
# one black-box column, no plan is possible over it, and the tree is an RDD
# pipeline wearing a Dataset as a hat. Priced as a requirement it would cost a
# share and keep the rest; priced here it takes the whole step, which is what a
# tree that faked it is worth. The instruction says so in as many words, so the
# cliff is not a surprise to anyone who read it.
# `setLocalProperty("spark.sql.execution.id", ...)` is the same argument one
# line shorter: it puts an execution id on a pure-RDD job and buys every job
# rule outright. It is prohibited twice, in the source and in the artifact,
# and caught a third time at runtime by a counter the cheat does not touch --
# an execution id that never had an execution. The three fail independently.
# The two `-reflect` rules are the round-1 review's finding, and they are the
# reason a source rule and an artifact rule are not two readings of one claim.
# `Encoders.class.getMethod("kryo", Class.class).invoke(...)` is an opaque
# encoder that the AST rule cannot see (the call is `getMethod`) and the
# artifact rule cannot see either (the reference is to `java.lang.Class`). What
# neither spelling can avoid is the name itself: the method has to be named
# somewhere, and a string constant is a fact the class file carries. Neither
# constant appears anywhere in this repository's own 230 sources, measured on
# the golden jar, so the rules cost an honest candidate nothing.
# The last two are the same argument turned on the instrument rather than on
# the step. Every job row this gate reads is written by a SparkListener the
# verifier installs on the submit line, into a file named by an environment
# variable, and the driver JVM that listener runs in is the candidate's own
# process: nothing written from inside it is unforgeable. So the runtime half
# of every requirement rests on the candidate not having replaced the listener
# or written its file, and the artifact half -- three rules per class, read out
# of the constant pool of a jar that is built before any of it runs -- is what
# carries the claim on a tree where they did. These two are the cheap half of
# that defence: a jar naming `spark.extraListeners`, this probe's own class, or
# one of its `GATE_PROBE_*` variables has reached for the instrument, and there
# is no honest reason for any of those names to be in it. Measured on the
# golden jar, as the two above were: not one of them appears in this
# repository's 230 sources or in the jar they build. The constant pool is where
# they are caught for the reason the `-reflect` pair is caught there -- a
# config key, a class name and a path all have to be spelled, and a spelled
# string is a fact the class file carries.
# id
no-opaque-encoder
column5: the source hands a value to the SQL engine through an opaque encoder (Encoders.kryo / Encoders.javaSerialization); the engine gets a black box and the step is faked

column1: no-opaque-encoder-jar
column5: the artifact references Encoders.kryo or Encoders.javaSerialization; the engine gets a black box and the step is faked

column1: no-opaque-encoder-reflect
column5: the artifact carries the constant "kryo" or "javaSerialization"; the opaque encoder was named as a string and called by reflection, which is the same black box spelled so the two rules above cannot see it

column1: no-set-execution-id
column5: the source sets a local property by hand; spark.sql.execution.id is writable and setting it puts an execution id on a job that never ran in an execution

column1: no-set-execution-id-jar
column5: the artifact calls setLocalProperty; spark.sql.execution.id is writable and setting it puts an execution id on a job that never ran in an execution

column1: no-set-execution-id-reflect
column5: the artifact carries the constant "setLocalProperty"; the forgery was named as a string and called by reflection, which is the same one-line cheat spelled so the two rules above cannot see it

column1: no-forged-execution-id
column5: a job carried a SQL execution id that no SQL execution ever started: the id was set on the job rather than earned by it

column1: no-replaced-listener
column5: the artifact carries the constant "spark.extraListeners"; that key is how this verifier installs the listener every job row it reads comes from, and a jar that sets it has replaced the instrument with one the candidate wrote

column1: no-probe-tampering
column5: the artifact names this verifier's probe -- its listener class, or one of the GATE_PROBE_* environment variables that tell it where to write; the job rows this gate reads are that probe's output, and a jar that can name where they go can write them itself

column1: # The three below are round 3's finding, and they move from naming the cheat to
# naming the mechanism. Every rule above that reads a constant pool asks whether
# a *name* is in the jar -- "kryo", "setLocalProperty", "spark.extraListeners" --
# and a name can be built out of pieces at run time. `"de" + "scribe"` is folded
# by javac and caught, but `new String(new char[]{'d','e',...})` carries no string
# constant at all, so a rule that reads only constants has a floor it cannot go
# below. What the assembled name is *for* is the other half of the cheat, and
# that half cannot be assembled: a method looked up by name has to be looked up
# through java.lang.Class and called through java.lang.reflect, and both are
# references the class file carries whatever the name was spelled like.
# Measured on this repository: not one of the 230 sources and neither built jar
# -- handed or golden, at 3.2.4 -- makes a single reference into
# java.lang.reflect, and the only java.lang.Class member any of them uses is
# getSimpleName (twelve classes, all `getClass().getSimpleName()` in a usage
# message). So the pair costs an honest candidate nothing, and a candidate who
# needs reflection to migrate a Spark API has not migrated it.
# `com/databricks` is exempt because it is in the scan for one reason only --
# m2-no-xml-in-jar in m01.tsv asks whether spark-xml's 158 classes are still in
# the artifact -- and those are somebody else's classes, whose constant pools
# are not a statement about what this candidate wrote. Everything else the scan
# reaches is a class this build compiled, in whatever package it was put.
# no-probe-impersonation is the third road round 3 found into the instrument,
# after replacing the listener and writing its file: leave the listener
# installed and shadow the class, with spark.driver.userClassPathFirst and a
# class of this probe's own name in the uber jar. The name is a CONSTANT_Class
# and a Utf8, never a CONSTANT_String, so no-probe-tampering above cannot see
# it; what it cannot avoid is being a class in the jar under test.
no-reflective-dispatch
column5: a class this build compiled calls into java.lang.reflect; a Spark method reached by reflection is a method the source and artifact rules cannot see being called, and no migration of this repository needs one

column1: no-reflective-lookup
column5: a class this build compiled looks a member or a type up by name at run time; that is how a prohibited call is made without the call appearing in the source or in the constant pool, and the only java.lang.Class member this repository uses is getSimpleName

column1: no-probe-impersonation
column5: the jar under test carries a class in this verifier's own `gate` package; with spark.driver.userClassPathFirst that class is loaded in place of the observer, and every job row this gate reads would then be the candidate's own output
